description: Hello, Space Apps community! We are Firewall Point, a team of Systems Engineering students joining NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We enjoy solving real-world problems through software development, data analysis, and digital tools. For the MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge, we want to make wildfire patterns easier to understand. Join us if you enjoy collaboration and impact! We welcome teammates with experience or interest in satellite data, GIS, data visualization, and UX design.
summary:
Firewall Point turns 26 years of NASA fire detections into a single timeline people can actually trust. The problem: MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) don't count fire the same way. VIIRS sees about four times more hotspots, so raw data makes 2012 look like the year fires exploded, when it was really the year a sharper satellite arrived.

We built a "Ghost Satellite", a model that reads each VIIRS detection (its intensity and size) and estimates how many 1 km cells Aqua MODIS would have flagged. The result is a daily record from 2000 to today where the source sensor no longer matters. Tested out of sample against real Aqua data in 71 countries (2012–2022), it stays within 0.35% of the true total, and a classifier can barely tell it apart from the real thing. In Peru, the raw series jumps 4.7× around 2012; ours, 0.98×.

On top of that record, anyone can pick a place and see its monthly burning calendar, compare future scenarios, get Telegram alerts, or learn through short games for kids. With MODIS near the end of its life, this keeps the fire history comparable for farmers, emergency teams and researchers.
details:
Firewall Point is a bilingual web app built for the NASA Space Apps challenge Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. It turns NASA FIRMS observations dating back to 2000 into an interactive fire activity map and calendar covering 71 countries and territories. Users select an area and a period to find recurring fire seasons, identify unusually active months, compare the current month’s pace with historical patterns, and download the results. Live demo

How it works. VIIRS can detect smaller fires than MODIS, so combining raw detections can create an artificial jump in the historical record. Our Ghost Satellite model uses overlapping observations and features such as fire radiative power to estimate how many grid cells Aqua MODIS would have flagged. We combine estimates from the VIIRS satellites available each day and track gaps in coverage. In held-out blocks of years from 2012 to 2022, the model achieved 11.4% median absolute percentage error, compared with 13.1% for a simpler country-and-month adjustment, on country-months with at least 20 observed Aqua cell-days. NASA FIRMS · Methodology and validation

Benefits and intended impact. We want emergency responders and land managers to see where and when extra monitoring may be needed, researchers to compare seasons across the sensor transition, and communities to understand local fire patterns. Yacana, our bilingual guide, explains the selected area’s data in plain language. Interactive games teach satellite detection and fire prevention, while an illustrated scenario tool lets users explore possible effects of mitigation choices.

Tools and design decisions. We built the data pipeline and model in Python, with FastAPI, DuckDB, and Parquet for analysis and delivery. The interface uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Google Maps, and the app is deployed with Docker Compose. We considered differences in sensor resolution, overpass timing, cloud cover, and outages. The calendar measures observed fire activity. Field conditions and decisions about when to burn still require local information.
